transcript:
This is NPR News Now.
The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News, I'm Lakshmi Singh.
President Trump says he and Chinese President Xi Jinping
have agreed to joint guardrails
amid the race to develop artificial intelligence.
A notable acknowledgement about the risks
involved with the technology is NPR's Deepa Shivaram.
Trump briefed the press on this week's trip to China.
Talk of, quote, guardrails is a new move for Trump,
who's always been adamant that the technology
should not have any regulations
because it would hold the U.S. back
in the race against China on AI.
Now he says sometimes the technology can be too powerful.
Neither country has released any further information
on what those joint safeguards could look like
or how they would be implemented.
Trump also said he would continue to push
for the construction of data centers in the U.S.
and will penalize companies that build them outside the U.S.
Deepa Shivaram, NPR News, Washington.
Trump's also touting successful talks
with Russian leader Vladimir Putin,
who also took part in yesterday's
historic trilateral meeting with the U.S. and China.
At the White House today, Trump addressed questions
about Russia's war with Ukraine.
I held a bilateral meeting with President Putin from Russia,
clearly expressed his desire to see the war
between Russia and Ukraine and by diplomatic means.
But after the summit, Russia engaged in more attacks
against Ukraine with missiles and drones that damaged bridges
and caused water outages.
New data out today indicate a majority of U.S.
Republicans do not trust the results of the midterms.
NPR's Miles Parks reports that despite President Trump
initially accepting the results himself.
The new survey data from UC San Diego may be a reality check
for those wondering if Trump's brand of election denial
has run its course in American politics.
Trump, after all, conceded that Republicans
had lost the House and Senate this year.
He blamed the candidates themselves.
Still, just 46 percent of Republicans say
they felt the midterms were free and fair,
and just 52 percent said they had confidence
in the country's vote counting process.
After the 2024 election, which Trump won,
Republican confidence in vote counting
was 30 percentage points higher.
It is typical for supporters of a losing party
to have some doubts about the process,
but experts say the swings that Republican confidence
in recent years are outside the norm.
Miles Parks, NPR News, Washington.
-On its second day of trading,
the anthropic stock price fell to a low of around $83,
down roughly 12 percent,
a day after opening at more than $111 a share
in its Wall Street debut.
Bloomberg managing editor Michael Regan
assesses the post-IPO volatility
for anthropic in the wider market.
-I think there was a sense that if anthropic
was really warmly received in the stock market,
and if we saw those shares continue to rise
above that -- well above that IPO price, that it would sort of
give investors confidence in the rest of the AI
portion of the market, which really is almost everything
when it comes to the stock market these days.
-The Nasdaq has closed down more than 1,200 points.
It's NPR News.
A second federal judge is blocking the construction
of President Trump's triumphal arch in Washington.
In the latest case challenging Trump's projects,
the Arlington County Board in Northern Virginia,
just outside the nation's capital,
sued, claiming the 250-foot arch
would endanger public safety and make traffic worse.
Tributes are pouring in from around the world
for the Cincinnati Zoo's most famous resident,
Fiona "The Hippo" Dodd yesterday,
from member station WVXU
in Cincinnati, Tana Weingartner reports.
-As dusk fell, a pile of flowers and cards grew ever larger
at a hippo statue outside the Cincinnati Zoo.
-Jenna Herey brought a bouquet of roses.
She said she lost twin sons during a high-risk pregnancy
around the same time Fiona was born in 2017,
and Fiona became a beacon of hope for her family.
-I just felt the need to pay tribute to her
and to the hope that she gave us during a really,
really hard time.
-Fiona ate a hat about two weeks ago
that was accidentally tossed into her habitat
and was unable to pass it through her system
despite what the zoo describes
as a heroic effort by her care team.
For NPR News, I'm Tana Weingartner in Cincinnati.
-New honors have been announced today.
Harvey Mason, among the newest recipients
of the Jazz Masters Fellowship
from the National Endowment for the Arts,
Terry Gibbs and Larry Ridley,
are also 2027 recipients
being honored for their contribution to the arts.
This is "NPR News."
-This week on "Consider This," air travel, email, banking --
why, over the last week,
does it seem like all our technology is breaking?
-Sometimes when you're updating systems, we all know.
Things can go wrong.
And, you know, never attribute anything to malice,
which is adequately explained by incompetence.
-Why system upgrades in the era of AI might be to blame.

Trump says he discussed Ukraine war with Putin, but Russia kept attacking Ukraine
